title: Robert Farnon, the master of string writing
summary: Mandel calls Robert Farnon simply the best, the source of everything he stole, and also remembers Marion Evans, who left music.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So, say if we were to discuss…
You can’t compare him to Robert Farnon.
It’s definitely apples and oranges.
You can’t compare anyone to Robert Farnon. Robert Farnon is simply the best.
What do you hear in Farnon’s work that particularly appeals to you?
Everything I’ve stolen.
[laughs loud] You don’t mind if I tell Gene Lees these lines, he’s – I think he actually might have mailed, he did a three part jazz letter on Robert Farnon…
Well then you’ll read that in there…
Oh, okay.
I said my technique consists mostly of stealing everything that I heard of Robert Farnon’s that I could capture.
[laughs]
There’s a lot of stuff I couldn’t capture.
How about Marion Evans?
Great arranger, I’m sorry he gave up music.
I don’t think he is.
He gave it up a long long time ago.
Yeah.
And he’ll never go back. I had dinner with him recently, he hasn’t been in music since the early 60s, or the late 50s, he became just a wizard at computers and the stock market.
And has done very very well for himself.
Oh yeah, yeah, but boy could he write. But there was still only one Governor, Robert Farnon.
Do you know him personally?
He’s the one that showed us all how.
Do you know him personally?
No, I’ve never met him but I’ve spoken to him on the phone.
What do you hear in his approach that you think appeals to so many writers?

He makes strings sound like they always should have sounded. He knows how to wrench at me, I personally respond a great deal to what he does, his choices of everything, his harmonic choices. I can only speak of my own experience, I don’t know about what the other writers hear, but they probably hear the same things I like.
I would say so.
It’s a none-sensational approach, it’s totally the opposite of Michel’s, he never goes for shock or for effect.
I was going to use the word, “sober,” to describe him as opposed to Michel’s which is as you call it, “flashy.”
Michel is very flamboyant, Bob is not flamboyant or flashy, but it’s so rich and it’s, I don’t know how to describe it, it’s very sensuous the way he writes.
And his uses of woodwinds of course.
